tasks.name: Search ordered data with explicit boundaries
Search monotonic boundaries and answer spaces
Use sorting and ordered scans deliberately

concepts.name: Exact binary search
concepts.description: Search ordered data by comparing the midpoint and discarding the half that cannot contain the target.

concepts.name: Boundary binary search
concepts.description: Search for the first/last position satisfying a monotonic condition while preserving a candidate interval invariant.

concepts.name: Binary-search interval and progress
concepts.description: Keep interval semantics explicit and update boundaries so the candidate region strictly shrinks without discarding possible answers.

concepts.name: Binary search on answer space
concepts.description: Search a numeric or ordered answer domain when a feasibility predicate changes monotonically from false to true or true to false.

concepts.name: Sort to expose structure
concepts.description: Pay sorting cost when ordered data makes later comparisons, grouping, merging, or scanning substantially simpler.

concepts.name: Sort key and comparator contract
concepts.description: Choose a sort key/comparison that matches the problem's intended ordering without discarding required metadata.

concepts.name: Stable ordering
concepts.description: Preserve prior relative order among equal-key records when tie order is part of the contract or a multi-stage sort.

concepts.name: Ordered merge scan
concepts.description: Combine or compare sorted sequences by advancing only the frontier that can produce the next ordered result.

questions.prompt: Implement `binary_search(values, target)`. `values` is sorted ascending. Return any index containing `target`, or `-1` if it is absent.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Compare the midpoint and discard the half that cannot contain the target. Every non-match update must shrink the candidate interval.
hints: Use an inclusive `[left, right]` interval.
Move past `mid` after a failed comparison.

questions.prompt: Repair `binary_search`. The current update can repeat the same midpoint forever when `mid == left`.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: When `values[mid] < target`, index `mid` is proven impossible, so `left` must become `mid + 1` to preserve correctness and guarantee progress.

questions.prompt: Implement `lower_bound(values, target)`. Return the first index whose value is `>= target`. Return `len(values)` if no such index exists.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Boundary search keeps the first possible answer instead of returning on equality. A half-open interval `[left, right)` is especially convenient.
hints: Do not stop at an arbitrary equal element.
When `values[mid] >= target`, keep `mid` as a possible answer by moving `right = mid`.

questions.explanation: This is the boundary where `value > target` first becomes true. Equality belongs on the left side of the boundary.

questions.explanation: At every midpoint, at least one half is normally sorted. Use that ordered half to decide whether the target can be discarded with the midpoint.

questions.explanation: The insertion position is exactly the lower bound: the first index whose value is at least the target.

questions.prompt: Complete `lower_bound(values, target)`. `values` is sorted ascending. Return the FIRST index whose value is greater than or equal to `target`; if every value is smaller, return `len(values)`. Examples: `lower_bound([10, 20, 20, 30], 20) -> 1`, `lower_bound([10, 20, 20, 30], 25) -> 3`, and target 40 returns 4. The search uses a half-open candidate interval `[left, right)`. When `values[mid] >= target`, `mid` might already be the first valid position and must remain a candidate. When `values[mid] < target`, `mid` is definitely too small and must be excluded. Fill both boundary updates.
questions.explanation: `mid` remains a candidate when its value already satisfies the boundary. When it is too small, `mid` itself is impossible and must be discarded.
hints: A midpoint that satisfies the boundary condition might be the answer, so keep it inside the search interval.
A midpoint that is too small cannot be the answer, so move the left boundary past it.

questions.prompt: Implement `min_eating_speed(piles, hours)`. At integer speed `k`, one pile of size `p` takes `ceil(p/k)` hours. Return the minimum positive integer speed that finishes all piles within `hours`.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: Feasibility is monotonic: once a speed is fast enough, every larger speed is also fast enough. Binary-search the first feasible speed.
hints: Search between 1 and `max(piles)`.
Compute hours with integer ceiling division `(p + k - 1) // k`.

questions.prompt: Implement `min_ship_capacity(weights, days)`. Packages must be shipped in the given order. A ship with capacity `c` takes a new day before adding a package that would exceed `c`. Return the minimum capacity that ships all packages within `days`.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: A capacity smaller than the largest package is impossible; the total weight always works. Feasibility changes monotonically from false to true as capacity increases.
hints: Lower bound: `max(weights)`. Upper bound: `sum(weights)`.
Write a helper that counts required days for one capacity.

questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: As the divisor grows, every ceiling quotient stays the same or decreases, so the total score is monotonic. Search for the first passing divisor.
hints: Search from 1 through `max(values)`.

questions.prompt: Implement `min_largest_partition_sum(values, parts)`. `values` contains non-negative integers. Split it into exactly `parts` non-empty contiguous groups. Minimize the largest group sum.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: For a proposed maximum sum `limit`, greedily forming a new group only when necessary tells whether the array can fit in at most `parts` groups. Larger limits never make feasibility worse.
hints: Search between `max(values)` and `sum(values)`.
Feasible with at most `parts` groups means you can split further, if necessary, to reach exactly `parts` because values are non-negative and groups are non-empty.

questions.prompt: Implement `min_days_for_bouquets(bloom_day, bouquets, adjacent)`. On day `d`, flowers with `bloom_day[i] <= d` are usable. Each bouquet needs `adjacent` consecutive unused usable flowers. Return the minimum day to make `bouquets` bouquets, or `-1` if impossible.
questions.instruction: Write or repair the function, run the tests, then submit.
questions.explanation: If bouquets are possible by day `d`, they remain possible on every later day. That gives a first-feasible-day boundary.
hints: Reject immediately if `bouquets * adjacent > len(bloom_day)`.
For one day, scan consecutive bloomed flowers and reset the run when an unavailable flower appears.

questions.prompt: Complete `first_feasible(low, high, feasible)`. The integer predicate is monotonic over the inclusive answer range: it looks like `False, False, ..., True, True`, and `high` is guaranteed feasible. Return the FIRST value for which `feasible(x)` is True. Example: if `feasible(x)` means `x >= 7` and the search range is 1 through 10, the answer must be 7. When the midpoint is feasible, it might be the first feasible value and therefore must stay in the candidate interval. When it is infeasible, the answer must be strictly to its right. Fill the two updates.
questions.explanation: A feasible midpoint may be the first feasible value, so it stays. An infeasible midpoint cannot be the answer and is discarded.
hints: A passing midpoint remains a possible first passing value.
A failing midpoint can be discarded together with everything below it.

questions.prompt: Complete `merge_sorted(a, b)`. Both input lists are already sorted ascending. Return one sorted list containing every input element in O(len(a) + len(b)) time. Example: `merge_sorted([1, 3, 5], [2, 4, 6]) -> [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]`. While both lists still have values, compare their current frontiers. The branch shown has already appended exactly one frontier, so only the pointer belonging to THAT consumed input should advance. Fill the two pointer updates.
questions.explanation: After emitting one frontier, advance only the input that supplied it. The other frontier still has not been consumed.
hints: Appending `a[i]` consumes one element from a and none from b.
